newsitem.title: KENYA: E.Africa seen offering untapped coffee potential.
newsitem.headline: E.Africa seen offering untapped coffee potential.

text.p: East African countries could increase their coffee output up to four times if they joined forces and shared information on vital issues related to production, Ted Lingle, president of the Specialty Coffee Association of America, said.
"If the countries are able to pull together and especially enlist the potential of Ethiopia, there is a real good potential for them to become a significant market player.
"The East African countries have the labour base and the land area, they are under-capitalised and would need some long-term investment, but the possibility is there," Lingle told Reuters.

Lingle, representing a leading U.S. coffee organisation whose members buy some three million 60-kg bags of high-quality and gourmet coffee a year, was speaking at the end of a coffee conference in Nairobi.
"If they...cooperate on how to improve husbandry and raise yields, they could easily double output, if not quadruple total output. Just basic husbandry could improve yields considerably," he said.
The average yield in Eastern Africa was only some 200 kg per hectare, which compared with levels well above one tonne per hectare in some Latin American and Asian countries.
Lingle said increased labour costs in particular in Central American countries in recent years were putting limits to how long they would remain important market players.
"As Central America industrialises it's becoming a lot more difficult for them to remain big producers. The major problem is rising labour costs, but also the land in becoming a problem.
"With more efforts for cooperation in East Africa there is an enormous potential for East Africa to become an important market factor of producers of good-quality mild arabica coffees," Lingle said.
Ethiopia and Uganda are the biggest coffee growers in East Africa with productions of between 3.5 and 4.0 million 60-kg bags of arabica and robusta coffee respectively.

Kenya produces in the range of 1.4 million bags of high-quality mild washed arabica coffee. Tanzania produces some 800,000 bags of mostly mild arabicas, while Burundi and Rwanda produces smaller quantities of mild arabicas.
